title: Ways to God (CCC 31–38)
hook: from the world and from the human person, reason can reach toward God

segments.voice: Yesterday, year four opens, with four pillars, the Catechism's floor plan. Your line was believe, celebrate, live, pray. Which of the four did your day lean on? Today, the first pillar opens. Day one thousand sixty-three.

Why is there a dandelion growing out of a crack in the parking lot? Not how. A botanist can tell you how. Why is there anything at all? A child might ask it out loud, at an inconvenient moment. The Catechism, opening its part on what Catholics believe, starts with that kind of question. Before scripture, before the Church, it asks: can a person, simply by looking at the world and at themselves, find a path that leads toward God? Today: ways to God.
screen: `A DANDELION IN A CRACK.` → `NOT HOW, BUT WHY?` → `A PATH TOWARD GOD?`

segments.voice: The Catechism doesn't call these proofs, the way a geometry problem has a proof. It calls them ways: paths of approach. And it says they offer converging and convincing arguments. Converging, like trails climbing a mountain from different sides toward the same summit. It names two starting points. First, the world. Movement and change, things coming to be, the order and the beauty of it all. Paul writes in Romans, in the Douay-Rheims, "the invisible things of him, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made." The Catechism adds Augustine, who tells his listeners to question the beauty of the earth, the sea and the sky. They all answer: look, we are beautiful. But their beauty changes. Who made them, Augustine asks, if not the Beautiful One who does not change? Second, the human person. Openness to truth and beauty. A sense of right and wrong that won't switch off. Freedom. The voice of conscience. A longing for a happiness nothing here quite fills. The Catechism calls the soul a seed of eternity in us. Then it's honest about limits. Catholic teaching holds that reason can come to know that God exists. But these ways don't hand anyone God in full; they point, they don't arrive. And the Catechism admits that in practice the human mind finds these truths hard, gets distracted, and is easily persuaded that what it would rather not be true is false or doubtful. That's why, it says, God also chose to speak, which is tomorrow's step. So the carry is converging clues. Not one knockout blow. Several quiet arrows, from the world and from inside us, pointing the same way.
screen: `WAYS, NOT PROOFS.` · `FROM THE WORLD: QUESTION ITS BEAUTY.` · `FROM THE PERSON: A SEED OF ETERNITY.` · `THEY POINT; THEY DON'T ARRIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at one thing and ask why it exists. Pick something within reach. A cup. Your own hand. A leaf outside the window. The light coming in. Settle, and breathe. Look at it as if you'd never seen one before. Notice its color, its edges, how it's put together. Then ask the old question, slowly: why is there this, and not nothing? Don't rush to an answer. Let the question sit in the room with you. If you pray, you can let the question turn toward God. If you don't, simply stay with the wonder. The bell holds the time.
Ways to God. Paths of approach, from the world and from the human person, that the Catechism calls converging and convincing. Today's word.
Your line: converging clues. Today, catch one thing that seems to point past itself, a bit of beauty, a pang of conscience, a longing, and just name it to yourself. Day one thousand sixty-three.

what a scholar hears: the Catechism's 'converging and convincing arguments', from movement, becoming, order and beauty, and from conscience and longing, with Romans 1:20 and Augustine's sermon on the beauty of the earth.
